summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would replace broadcasting licence fees and datacasting charges with a new tax on transmitter licences for commercial broadcasters.
The tax would apply to each individual transmitter linked to an apparatus licence, with the minister setting the amount up to a cap specified in the bill.
The tax would take effect from 1 July 2017, but only if the related reform bill also passes.
changes: Abolishes broadcasting licence fees and datacasting charges.
Introduces a transmitter licence tax for use of broadcast spectrum.
Aligns tax arrangements for commercial broadcasters with those of other commercial spectrum users.
summary.affected: Commercial free-to-air broadcasters holding transmitter licences under the Radiocommunications Act 1992.

The majority voted in favour of [adjourning the debate](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-09-11.217.1) and so put off further discussion on these bills until a later time. ### What do the bills do? The two bills are the: * [Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5907); and the * [Commercial Broadcasting (Tax) Bill 2017](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5908). Most significantly, the bills were introduced to get rid of certain media ownership, control and diversity laws, like the ‘75% audience reach rule’, which stops commercial television broadcasting licensees from controlling licences if the combined licence area has a population over 75% of Australia' population. It would also get rid of the ‘2 out of 3 cross-media control rule’, which stops a company from having control over more than two out of three regulated media platforms in any one commercial radio licence area. Read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd08).

The majority supported continuing their discussion of the bill [on the next sitting day](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-09-11.219.1). In other words, they agreed to resume debate the next time they were sitting in the Senate. ### What do the bills do? The two bills are the: * [Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5907); and the * [Commercial Broadcasting (Tax) Bill 2017](http://parlinfo.aph.gov.au/parlInfo/search/display/display.w3p;query=Id:legislation/billhome/r5908). Read more in the [bills digest](https://www.aph.gov.au/Parliamentary_Business/Bills_Legislation/bd/bd1718a/18bd08).

The majority voted in favour of a [motion](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-09-13.191.1): > *That if by 7.20 pm today, the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment (Broadcasting Reform) Bill 2017 and the Commercial Broadcasting (Tax) Bill 2017 have not been finally considered then:* > > *(a) the routine of business from not later than 7.20 pm shall be consideration of the bills listed above; and* > > *(b) the Senate shall adjourn without debate after it has finally considered the bills or at 11 pm, whichever is the earlier.*

The majority voted in favour of an [amendment](http://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2017-09-13.212.20) introduced by WA Senator [Rachel Siewert](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/wa/rachel_siewert) (Greens). The amendment changes the second motion text - which is normally "*That these bills be now read a [second time](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html)*" - by adding: > *"but the Senate is of the opinion that all free-to-air television broadcasters should use the financial relief afforded by the reduction in licensing fees to offer audio description services for people who are blind or vision-impaired, and ensure provisioning of captioning services on all broadcast programs aligning thus with the National Disability Strategy 2010-2020, which calls for all broadcast programs to be fully captioned".* This change doesn't have any legal affect - that is, it won't force the Government to do what it asks for. However, it does have political influence in that it represents the will of the Senate. ### What does it mean to read the bills "a second time"? There are [several stages](https://www.peo.gov.au/learning/fact-sheets/making-a-law.html) that a bill must pass through before becoming law. When the Senate is asked to read a bill for the "second time", it means that they are being asked whether they agree with the main idea of the bill. speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: The Commercial Broadcasting (Tax) Bill 2017 introduces a new spectrum tax to replace broadcasting licence fees, raising about $40 million annually and providing overall fee relief for broadcasters, with regional broadcasters paying significantly less based on transmitter power and spectrum use. The bill is part of the government's Broadcast and Content Reform Package, has unanimous industry support, and is contingent on the passage of the Broadcasting Reform Bill.

speeches.speaker: Michelle Rowland
speeches.brief: Labor supported the majority of the broadcasting reform bills but opposed repealing the two-out-of-three cross-media rule, warning it would worsen Australia’s already high media ownership concentration and harm diversity, and criticised the government’s piecemeal approach for lacking holistic, evidence-based reform.

speeches.speaker: Paul Fletcher
speeches.brief: The government argued that the Broadcasting Legislation Amendment Bill 2017 and Commercial Broadcasting (Tax) Bill 2017 will abolish broadcasting licence fees, introduce a spectrum tax, and remove the 75% audience reach rule and two-out-of-three rule while maintaining protections for local content and competition, with the package having unanimous media industry support.
